title: The Seventh Child Is Drawn Away
story:
Devaki had been with child seven times, and every child that had come from her had been taken from her arms and dashed against a stone. Each birth in that prison had ended the same way, in Kamsa's cruelty, and still the seventh child was growing within her now, while Kamsa's servants waited for it the way they had waited for all the others. But this child would not reach their hands. There was a plan for this one, laid in a place Kamsa could not see, and it was already unfolding in the dark.

For while the world kept its watch, a quiet work was being done. The embryo of Devaki's seventh conception was drawn, by a hidden power, out of her womb and carried into another — into the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's other wife, who waited far from the prison and knew nothing of it. Not a sound was made, and no one saw it done.

Rohini felt only the sign of it, and the sign was a frightening one. At the dead of night, while she lay in a deep sleep, a flow of blood came, and what felt like the loss of the child within her. In her dream she saw the embryo slipping away from her, and in the dream she reached out to hold it and could not; when she woke she reached again and found it gone. In that dark hour, Vasudeva's wife Rohini, lovely as the moon, was seized with grief, certain that the child she carried had been taken from her.

Then, out of the darkness, a voice spoke — the goddess of sleep herself, who had done this thing. O fair one, she said, do not grieve. I have drawn the embryo out of Devaki's womb and placed it in yours. This son of yours will be celebrated by the name Sankarshana.

The name meant the one drawn out — drawn from one mother into another, carried from the prison where Kamsa's men waited into the safety of a house that no one was watching. The child who had seemed lost in the night had not been lost at all; he had been moved, the way a lamp is moved from a dark room into a lit one. And at the goddess's words the fear went out of Rohini. She understood, and she was glad. The grief that had seized her an hour before loosened its hold, and what had looked like the end of everything became, in a breath, a beginning.

Pleased, and quiet now, she bowed her head and returned to her house, the way the beautiful wife of the moon walks with her light hidden. Within her grew the child who would one day be known as Balarama — the first of the two brothers, the one who would come before the other and clear the way. In a prison, Kamsa's men went on watching an empty womb and did not know it. In a quiet house, the seventh child slept on, safe. The eighth child would come soon enough, and with him the storm; but for now, in that quiet house, there was only this one small saved life, breathing in the dark.
reflection: The seventh child is saved not by strength but by concealment — drawn from one womb to another under cover of night, while the world and its watchers slept. Rohini's night of blood and grief, which looked like loss, was the very sign of the child's deliverance, and her fear turned to joy in a single sentence from the dark.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana also tells of this transfer; the working is elsewhere described as the command of the divine power Yogamaya, who draws the embryo from Devaki into Rohini so the child may be born beyond Kamsa's reach.
content_note: Rohini briefly believes she has lost her child in the night; the loss is only apparent, and the story ends in comfort.
next_story_tease: And after this quiet rescue, Kamsa would do the one thing no one expected — and Devaki would forgive him for it.
hero_scene: Rohini waking in the dead of night, moonlit and frightened, as the goddess of sleep speaks from the darkness to tell her the child has been drawn from Devaki's womb into her own and will be called Sankarshana.
visual_elements: the goddess of sleep speaking unseen
mood of grief turning to wonder and relief
